BDL and BAF airports show the highest total potentials—519 and 436 MMgge/yr3, respectively—while Massachusetts airports dominate overall. Across all locations, MSW (up to 2,311 MMgge/yr) and FOG (up to 375 MMgge/yr) represent nearly 80% of total resources, highlighting urban waste streams as key feedstocks. Spatially, most bioenergy potential is captured within 5–50 miles of each airport nonlinearly, indicating that local collection systems are both efficient and sustainable. Regional patterns show MSW and FOG dominance in urban areas and woody biomass strength in Maine. These findings suggest that developing airport-centered biorefineries—particularly near BDL, BAF, ORH, and BOS—could enhance sustainable aviation fuel production, leverage waste recovery infrastructure, and support New England’s transition toward a circular, low-carbon energy economy. New England’s Jet A is primarily sourced from New York Harbor and Canadian imports. The relative volumes sourced from these two areas can shift based on fuel availability, price, tariffs and other factors. Figure ES-1 shows jet fuel flows in New England and the location of refineries, terminals storing Jet A, and airports selected for the study. Large volumes of Jet A are delivered on the Colonial Pipeline from the Texas to New York Habor terminals, where the fuel is offloaded to barges and tankers for delivery to New England terminals. Irving Oil’s New Brunswick refinery supplies New England terminals by barge and tanker. Jet fuel movements by pipeline in the region are limited. BOS receives fuel that is delivered by barge to Energy Transfer’s East Boston terminal, where it is then delivered by pipeline to the airport.
